check:0:0.q: Why not “Yes: it times every request”?
check:0:0.a:
"Yes: it times every request" sounds reasonable. It gets one thing right: a batch does send every request in your set, so it covers them all.

But what you want here is speed. **Time to first words** means how long a person waits before the answer starts to appear. **p95** is the time that 95 out of 100 requests beat, so it shows the slow end of what people feel.

A batch can't give you that. Each batch answer waited in a queue before the model got to it. So any time you take from a batch includes that waiting, and nobody using your app would feel that wait. The whole job aims for 24 hours and often takes minutes, but that tells you nothing about how quickly one answer starts when someone is waiting for it.

That's why the lesson says to time a small **inline sample** for speed (one call at a time, timed as it happens) and send the rest as a batch.

"No: batch answers waited in a queue first" is better because it names the reason: queue time gets mixed into every batch answer, so batch timings can't show what a waiting person feels.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. It is slightly over 200 words, and 'covers them all' is loose given the lesson says some requests fail or never come back, but it only claims they were all sent.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Only if the job finishes within an hour”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. It senses that waiting time spoils the measurement. But it puts the problem in the wrong place.

First, some jargon. "Time to first words" is how long a person waits before the model starts replying. "p95" means the time that 95 out of 100 requests beat. It is the slow end that users notice.

How fast the whole job finishes doesn't change what each answer went through. A job that finishes in an hour, or in five minutes, still parked every request in a queue first. Its timings mix queue wait with model work, and you can't pull them apart. A batch also doesn't stream words to you as they're written. You get finished answers in a file, so there is no "first words" moment to time at all.

So a fast job is still the wrong tool for speed. Time a small inline sample for that, and batch the rest.

"No: batch answers waited in a queue first" is better because it names the real reason. No batch timing reflects what a waiting person feels, however quickly the job ends.

judge.notes: No real problems. The streaming remark (batch gives no 'first words' moment) goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Wait: it will expire on its own”?
check:1:0.a:
"Wait: it will expire on its own" gets one thing right. A batch is for work nobody is waiting on, so a bit of patience is normal. A slow job is not a crisis.

But the key idea is wrong. On Foundry, the 24 hours is a **target**, not a deadline. A target is the time it aims for. A deadline is when it would be forced to stop. Missing the target does not end the job. A late job keeps running until **you** cancel it. So waiting for it to expire means waiting for something that won't happen. Meanwhile, the 700 finished answers sit unused, and the 300 slow ones may stay stuck.

Cancelling is safe because it hands back only what finished. You lose nothing that was done. Then you match each answer to its request by `custom_id`, the label each request carries. The requests with no answer are the **leftovers**. You send those in a fresh job.

"Cancel it, keep the 700, send the 300 again" is better because you keep the finished work now and give the unfinished part a new chance to complete.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Send all 1,000 again as a new job”?
check:1:2.a:
"Send all 1,000 again" gets one thing right: a fresh job gives every request another chance. Nothing slips through the cracks.

But it misses two things.

First, 700 requests already have answers. Sending them again means you pay for that work twice. You also make the new job much bigger than it needs to be.

Second, it ignores the old job. On Foundry, the 24 hours is a target, not a deadline. A late job keeps running until you **cancel** it, which means telling Foundry to stop the job. So if you never cancel, you now have two jobs running, both working on the same requests.

The lesson's pattern is cleaner. Cancelling returns only what finished. You match those answers to their requests by `custom_id`. Then you send just the **leftovers**, the requests with no answer, as a new job.

"Cancel it, keep the 700, send the 300 again" is better because it stops the stuck job, keeps the work you already paid for, and pays only for the 300 that still need answers.

check:2:0.q: Why not “By position: line 1 is request 1”?
check:2:0.a:
Matching by position feels natural. It's how inline calls work: you send one request, you get its answer, and the pairing is obvious. Your request file is also in order, so it seems fair to expect the output to follow.

But a batch doesn't keep that order. The service works on many requests at once, and each answer is written down when it finishes. So line 1 of the output might be the answer to request 40.

There's a second problem. Some requests fail, and some never come back at all, for example if the job was cancelled. That leaves gaps. With position matching, one missing answer shifts every line after it. Request 5 gets request 6's answer, and so on down the file. You'd pair the wrong questions with the wrong answers, and nothing would warn you.

You also couldn't tell which requests are missing, so you wouldn't know which leftovers to send again.

"By each line's `custom_id`" is better because each answer carries the label of its own request, so it matches correctly no matter the order or how many went missing.

check:2:2.q: Why not “By the length of each answer”?
check:2:2.a:
Matching by length sounds clever, but nothing ties an answer's length to its request.

**What it gets right:** it notices that you need *some* clue on each answer to pair it with its request, because the order can't be trusted.

**What it misses:**

- **You don't know the length ahead of time.** The model writes the answer. You can't predict that request `q1` will produce 412 characters.
- **Lengths repeat.** Two answers can easily be the same length, or close. Then you can't tell which is which.
- **Failed requests break it.** A failed line has an error instead of an answer. There's no answer length to compare.
- **Missing answers stay hidden.** If a request never came back, length gives you no way to spot which one is gone. So you can't send the leftovers again.

A `custom_id` is a label you choose and attach to each request. The service copies it, unchanged, onto that request's line in the output.

**Why `custom_id` is better:** it's a unique label you set yourself, and it comes back on every result line, answered or failed, so each one points to exactly one request.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The count is off.** You sent 500 requests but scored only 470 answers. The score can look fine, because the missing ones simply aren't counted. Some failed, and some never came back.
- **Answers don't fit their questions.** The output comes back in any order. If answers were paired by position instead of by `custom_id`, an answer about refunds may sit next to a question about shipping. Scores then look oddly random or low.
- **Speed numbers look strange.** If speed was timed from the batch, you'll see minutes or hours per answer. That's time spent waiting in a queue (a waiting line on the server), not what a person feels. Speed should come from a small inline sample.
- **A job is still `in_progress` well past 24 hours.** It won't stop on its own. Cancelling gives you only what finished, so the rest need sending again.

**Quickest check**

Compare two numbers: requests sent, and `custom_id`s that came back with an answer. If they differ, you have leftovers to send again. Then read three or four answers next to their own questions, matched by `custom_id`, to confirm the pairing is right.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the method needs care.

**Someone is waiting.** A chat app or a live agent can't sit in a queue (a waiting line) for minutes or hours. Use inline calls there, and keep batches for work nobody is watching, like eval sets.

**Ids that aren't unique.** Matching only works if every `custom_id` points to exactly one request. If two requests share an id, you can't tell which answer belongs to which, so check for repeats before you build the file.

**Requests that fail every time.** Some requests break on every try, for example a prompt too long for the model to read. If you keep sending the leftovers again, the loop never ends. Set a limit on retries, then put the stubborn ones aside and look at them by hand.

learn:term.a:
In this lesson, the **batch** is *what* you send, and the **job** is *the work done on it*.

**The batch** is the bundle of requests. It's your `requests.jsonl` file: many questions, one per line, each with its own `custom_id`. On its own, it just sits there.

**The job** is the single piece of work the service runs on that bundle. It starts when you call `client.batches.create(...)`. It has its own `job.id` and a status that changes over time, like `validating`, `in_progress`, `completed`. You check on it with `client.batches.retrieve(job.id)`. You can also cancel it, and then you get back only what finished.

**How they fit together:** you hand over one batch, and one job processes it. If some requests fail or never come back, those leftovers become a new batch, sent as a new job.

**Everyday comparison:** a bag of laundry is the batch. The wash the laundromat runs on that bag is the job. The wash takes time, can be "still going" or "done," and can be stopped early with only part of the bag clean.

One naming catch: the SDK calls jobs `batches`.

check:0:0.q: Why not “No: it costs 10 times more per call”?
check:0:0.a:
The "No" answer gets one thing right. The new model really does cost 10 times more per call. That part is true.

What it misses is the size of the numbers. "10 times more" is a ratio, a comparison of two prices. It tells you nothing about the actual dollars. Ten times a tiny number is still a tiny number.

Work it out for every 100 tickets:

- **Extra cost:** 100 calls × ($0.02 − $0.002) = 100 × $0.018 = $1.80
- **Extra value:** 25 more resolved tickets × $4 = $100

So you pay about $1.80 more and earn $100 more. That leaves roughly $98.20 extra net value for every 100 tickets. Net value means what you earn minus what the calls cost.

The "No" answer looks only at the price. It ignores what the better success rate earns. That is exactly the trap this lesson warns about: judging a model by its price alone.

"Yes: the extra tickets are worth more" is better because it compares the actual dollars on both sides, and the $100 gained easily outweighs the $1.80 spent.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Can't tell without the monthly volume”?
check:0:2.a:
"Can't tell without the monthly volume" sounds careful, and it gets one thing right. Volume decides *how much* money you gain in total. At 10,000 tickets a month the gain is bigger than at 100.

But volume can't decide *whether* the switch is worth it. Every ticket gets both the extra value and the extra cost. So volume multiplies both sides by the same number, and the winner stays the same.

You can compare per 100 tickets instead:

- Extra value: 25 more resolved × $4 = $100.
- Extra cost: 100 calls × ($0.02 − $0.002) = 100 × $0.018 = $1.80.
- Net gain: about $98 for every 100 tickets.

Whatever the monthly volume is, it just scales that $98 up or down. The gain never flips to a loss. This is the lesson's point: a pricier model can pay for itself many times over.

"Yes: the extra tickets are worth more" is better because it compares the extra value with the extra cost for each ticket. That comparison alone settles the decision, whatever the volume.

check:1:0.q: Why not “How new each model is”?
check:1:0.a:
It's a fair thought. Newer models often do better, so "how new" hints at something real: quality matters, not just price.

But newness isn't part of the money sum. Net monthly value is what good answers earn minus what the calls cost:

- **Earned:** volume times success rate times value per success.
- **Cost:** volume times cost per call.

A model's release date appears nowhere in that. A brand-new model might be no better at *your* task than an older one. It might even be worse. Age is a guess about quality, not a measure of it. You could pick the newest model and still lose money if it succeeds less often on your requests.

The manager's "cheapest per call" idea only looks at the cost side. What it really leaves out is the earning side, and newness doesn't fill that gap. A measured success rate does. That's the number you'd log in MLflow (the tool that records each experiment run) as `success_rate`.

"How many good answers each gives" is the better answer because it is the success rate, the exact missing piece that decides how much each model earns.

judge.notes: No major problems. The claim that newer models often do better comes from outside the lesson, and the length is borderline at about 200 words.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Which one has more users”?
check:1:2.a:
"Which one has more users" points at something real. Volume, meaning how many calls you get each month, is part of the net value formula. More calls multiply both what you earn and what you pay.

But it doesn't help you choose between models. When you compare two models, they serve the same traffic. Both get the same `volume`, say 10,000 calls a month. So the number of users can't be what separates them.

The manager's "cheapest per call" rule leaves something else out. It looks only at the cost side. It ignores how often each model actually succeeds. A cheap model that gives bad answers earns little, because only good answers bring in `value_per_success`. A pricier model with a higher `success_rate` can earn far more than it costs.

"How many good answers each gives" is the better answer because success rate is the missing half of the formula, the earning side that the cheapest-per-call rule ignores.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the claim that both models serve the same traffic is an inference from the single shared volume in the lesson's formula, not something it states.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Model B: it gets more answers right”?
check:2:1.a:
That choice is tempting. Model B really is better at the task, and more right answers do earn more money. That part is true.

What it misses is the other half of the sum. Net monthly value means what the good answers earn, minus what the calls cost. A higher success rate only tells you about the first half.

Here, compare B to A:

- B's extra good answers earn **$50 more** a month.
- B's calls cost **$500 more** a month.

So switching to B changes your net by $50 − $500 = **−$450** a month. You would be paying $500 to get $50 back. Being right more often doesn't help if each extra right answer costs far more than it earns.

This is the lesson's big idea. Don't pick a model by its success rate alone, or by its price alone. Pick it by the money left over after paying for its calls.

**Model A: B's extra cost is bigger** is the better answer because it weighs the $50 gained against the $500 spent and sees that A leaves you $450 a month better off.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Neither: they come out the same”?
check:2:2.a:
"Neither: they come out the same" gets one thing right. It knows you have to weigh B's extra earnings against B's extra cost, instead of looking at just one side. That's the core habit of this lesson.

What it misses is the actual numbers. The two sides are not equal:

- B's extra good answers earn **$50** more a month.
- B's calls cost **$500** more a month.

Put together, B's net (what it earns minus what its calls cost) is $50 − $500 = **−$450** compared with A. So B leaves you $450 a month worse off. That's a clear gap, not a tie.

A tie would only happen if the extra earnings exactly matched the extra cost, say $500 and $500. Even then, the lesson's rule doesn't say "neither." It keeps the option listed first, because a new option has to be *strictly* bigger to replace the best one so far.

"Model A: B's extra cost is bigger" is better because it does the subtraction and sees that B's $500 extra cost swamps its $50 extra value, so A makes more money each month.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The pick always matches one number.** If the winner is always the cheapest model, or always the one with the highest success rate, only one side of the sum is being counted. The net needs both: what good answers earn and what all calls cost.
- **The money doesn't show up.** You ship a model with a great success rate, then the monthly bill eats the gains. Or you ship a cheap model and earnings drop because it fails more often.
- **Runs are missing the business inputs.** Your MLflow runs show `success_rate` and `cost_per_call`, but not `volume`, `value_per_success`, or a `net_monthly_value` metric. Then nobody can see later why a model was chosen.
- **The pick changes with list order when the nets differ.** That points to a comparison mistake. On an exact tie, though, the option listed first should win, so reordering tied options is expected to change the pick.

**Quickest check**

Take two options. Work out each net by hand with a calculator: volume × success rate × value per success, minus volume × cost per call. Then confirm the bigger one is the model you chose.

learn:stops.a:
The rule is simple, so the danger is in the numbers you feed it. Here are three places it needs extra care.

**Very little test data.** If you measured success on only 50 examples, a gap of a few percent may just be luck. Test on more examples, and treat close results as a tie rather than trusting a tiny edge.

**An LLM or RAG app.** With these, cost per call isn't fixed, because longer prompts, extra retrieved documents and retries all cost more. A wrong answer can also cost money, like a refund or an angry customer, so subtract a cost per failure too. (RAG means the app looks up documents and feeds them to the model before it answers.)

**Things change over time.** Volume grows, model prices drop, and users start asking different questions. Redo the calculation regularly with fresh numbers, logging each check as a new MLflow run so you can compare decisions over time.

learn:term.a:
Without this idea, teams pick models for the wrong reason. Some grab the cheapest one. Others grab the one with the best success rate. Both can lose money.

**A realistic example.** A support bot answers 10,000 questions a month. Each good answer saves about $4 of a human agent's time.

- **Cheap model:** 70% success, $0.01 per call.
  Earns 10,000 × 0.70 × $4 = $28,000. Costs 10,000 × $0.01 = $100. Net: **$27,900**.
- **Smart model:** 90% success, $0.20 per call.
  Earns $36,000. Costs $2,000. Net: **$34,000**.

The smart model costs 20 times more per call. Yet it makes $6,100 more every month. A team that only looked at price would pick the cheap one and never notice the loss.

The trap also runs the other way. A model with a slightly higher success rate but a huge price per call can earn less overall.

So the net is the fair way to compare. Net means earnings minus costs. It turns "which model is better?" into one number per option.

Logging that number in MLflow, the tool that records each experiment, means you can later show *why* you chose a model, not just *which* one.

check:0:0.a:
"Yes, for variety" has a sensible instinct behind it. Having more than one option can feel safer, and in real projects you sometimes do want a backup model.

But variety only helps if each option gives you something the others don't. Here, C gives you nothing. A is cheaper, faster and more accurate on the same eval set. So there is no situation where you would pick C over A. Whatever you care about most, quality, cost or speed, A wins.

That is exactly what the lesson means by A **dominating** C. A is at least as good on every measure and better on at least one. In this case, it's better on all three.

The shortlist is meant to hold only **real trade-offs**. Those are models where choosing one means giving something up, like paying more for better quality. Keeping C adds clutter and forces a decision that was never really a decision.

"No: A beats it on everything" is better because a model that another model beats on every measure can never be the right choice, so it doesn't belong on the shortlist.

check:0:2.a:
"Only if it's newer" has a sensible instinct behind it. Newer models often get better over time, and you might expect them to improve. So it feels risky to throw one away.

But the shortlist isn't built on hopes about a model. It's built on what you measured: quality, cost and p95 latency, all on the same eval set with the same judge. (p95 latency means 95% of answers come back at least this fast.)

On those three numbers, model C loses to model A every time. It's less accurate, more expensive and slower. Being newer doesn't change any of those results. A newer model that measures worse is still worse for this task, today.

If you think a newer version might improve, the right move is to re-run the eval when it does. Then let the new numbers decide.

"No: A beats it on everything" is the better answer because A dominates C on every measure that matters for the choice, so keeping C gives you no real trade-off to weigh.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Yes, drop Y: lower quality”?
check:1:0.a:
"Yes, drop Y: lower quality" gets one thing right. X really does beat Y on quality.

But the rule for throwing a model out is stricter. Model A beats model B only if A is at least as good on all three measures (quality, cost and p95 latency) and better on at least one. Here X loses on two of them: Y is cheaper and Y is faster. So X does not beat Y.

(p95 latency means 95 out of 100 answers come back at least this fast. Lower is better.)

Dropping Y looks at one number and ignores the other two. That throws away a real option. For your task, a small drop in quality might be fine if it saves money and time.

So neither model is thrown out. Both stay on the Pareto front, the short list of models nothing beats. Choosing between them is a trade-off, decided by what quality is worth to you.

"No, each one wins on something" is better because X wins on quality while Y wins on cost and speed, so neither model beats the other.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The one minor wobble is that 'X really does beat Y on quality' uses 'beat' loosely, before the strict meaning is given.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Yes, drop X: it costs more”?
check:1:1.a:
"Yes, drop X: it costs more" gets one thing right. Cost really does matter, and on cost, Y is the better model. X is also slower. So X loses on two of the three things we measure.

But losing on some things is not enough to throw a model out. The rule is stricter. A model only gets dropped when another model **beats** it. Beating means being at least as good on quality, cost and latency, and better on at least one. ("Latency" just means how long you wait for an answer.)

Y does not beat X. Y is cheaper and faster, but X has higher quality. So neither model beats the other. Both stay on the short list, and that list is the **Pareto front**: the models nothing beats.

Dropping X for costing more skips the real question. Is the extra quality worth the extra cost and wait? For some tasks it is. For others it isn't. That choice is yours, not the rule's.

"No, each one wins on something" is better because it applies the rule correctly: X and Y each have a strength the other lacks, so this is a real trade-off, not a clear loser.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Nothing, B simply scored higher”?
check:2:0.a:
"Nothing, B simply scored higher" gets one thing right. B's number really is higher. That part is true.

What it misses is *why* B's number is higher. B answered easier questions. An easy test makes almost any model look good. So the higher score might come from the questions, not from the model. You can't tell which.

Think of two students. One sits a hard exam and gets 70%. The other sits an easy quiz and gets 90%. You can't say the second student is smarter. They didn't take the same test.

That's why the lesson says to run every candidate on the **same eval set** (the fixed list of test questions) with the **same judge** (the scorer that grades each answer, like `Correctness()`). Only then is a difference in score caused by the models themselves. It's also why each model gets its own MLflow run with the same `eval_set`. The runs are then fair to put side by side.

"They weren't tested the same way" is better because it names the real flaw: a score gap means nothing unless both models faced the same questions and the same grader.

judge.notes: No significant problems. Minor overreach: 'only then is a difference caused by the models' and 'means nothing' are a bit absolute, but they fit the lesson's same-eval-set, same-judge point.

check:2:2.q: Why not “A should get a second try”?
check:2:2.a:
"A should get a second try" has a fair instinct behind it. A's lower score might not be A's fault, so A shouldn't be written off yet.

But a second try only helps if it changes the setup. If A simply runs again on its own harder set, the problem is still there. A is graded on hard questions, and B is graded on easy ones. B's higher score could come from the easier questions, not from being a better model.

The real issue is the test, not A's luck. The fix is to put both models on the same eval set, with the same judge. An eval set is the fixed list of test questions. The judge is the scorer that grades the answers, like `Correctness()`. You could rerun A on B's set, or run both on one new set. Either works, because the conditions now match. That is why the lesson logs one MLflow run per model on the same `eval_set`.

"They weren't tested the same way" is the better answer because it names the actual flaw: different test conditions, so the scores can't be fairly compared.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs in your results**

- **A model that loses on everything is still on the shortlist.** It has lower quality, higher cost and slower p95 latency than another model, yet it survives. A common cause is a flipped direction. Quality should be high, but cost and latency should be low.
- **A clear favourite gets thrown out**, even though no single model matches or beats it on all three numbers.
- **Two models with identical numbers vanish.** Neither is better on anything, so neither beats the other. Both should stay.

**Warning signs in your MLflow runs**

- Runs show different numbers of eval rows, or different scorers. The comparison isn't fair.
- A "winner" scores well in testing, then disappoints in real use. Check it was run on the same eval set as the others.

A long shortlist is not a warning sign. It can simply mean real trade-offs.

**Quickest check**

Pick one dropped model and name the model that beats it. Confirm by eye that the winner is at least as good on all three numbers and better on one. Then pick one kept model and confirm no other model does that to it.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where the "throw out any model another model beats" rule needs extra care.

**A small or noisy eval set.** With only a few dozen questions, a quality score of 0.80 versus 0.78 can be pure luck. Grow the eval set, or run it twice, and treat close scores as a tie before deciding one model `beats` another.

**Numbers that change over time.** Prices drop, latency shifts with traffic, and a model service can quietly switch to a newer version. Rerun the comparison on a schedule and log each round as fresh MLflow runs, so old results don't decide today's choice.

**Thousands of candidates.** Comparing every model with every other is fine for five models, but the number of comparisons explodes as the list grows. First cut the list with simple limits, like a top cost you'll accept or a lowest quality you'll accept. Then compare what's left.

learn:term.q: How is “same eval set” different from “same judge”?
learn:term.a:
They fix two different things. Both need to stay the same so the only thing that changes is the model.

**Same eval set** means the same questions. An eval set is a fixed list of test inputs, often with the answers you expect. Every model answers exactly these.

**Same judge** means the same grader. A judge is whatever scores each answer. Here it is `Correctness()`, a scorer that checks if an answer is right. Every model's answers get marked by it.

Think of two students sitting an exam. They need the same exam paper (eval set). They also need the same marker (judge). Give one student an easier paper, and the scores mean nothing. Give one a stricter marker, and you have the same problem.

In the lesson's example, look at what stays fixed inside the loop:

```python
mlflow.genai.evaluate(data=eval_set, predict_fn=make_app(model), scorers=[Correctness()])
```

`data=eval_set` keeps the questions the same. `scorers=[Correctness()]` keeps the grader the same. Only `make_app(model)` changes on each pass. So any difference in quality comes from the model alone.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Everything feels fast: the average is 900 ms”?
check:0:0.a:
The 900 ms figure is real. The model's average latency really is 900 ms. But "everything feels fast" claims more than an average can tell you.

An average blends every request into one number. A few very slow requests can hide inside it, as long as many others are quick. So the average alone can't tell you whether every request is fast.

The p95 shows what the average hides. A p95 of 4 seconds means 95 out of 100 requests finish within 4 seconds. The other 5 out of 100 take longer than that. Four seconds is more than four times the average. So those requests are slow, and the users who send them feel the wait.

That is why teams compare models and configs (their settings) on p95, not on the average. The p95 points to the slow requests that the average blends away.

"About 1 in 20 requests feels slow" is the better answer because 5 out of 100 is 1 in 20, and it describes the slow requests that the p95 reveals and the average hides.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Every request takes about 900 ms”?
check:0:2.a:
"Every request takes about 900 ms" reads the average as if it were a promise for each request. It isn't.

**What it gets right:** the average really is 900 ms. Most requests are probably fast, maybe well under a second.

**What it misses:** an average blends fast and slow requests into one number. A few very slow ones get hidden by many quick ones. Picture nine requests at 500 ms and one at 4,500 ms. The average is 900 ms, yet that one user waited four and a half seconds.

The p95 tells you about that spread. A p95 of 4 seconds means 95 out of 100 requests finish in 4 seconds or less. So the slowest 5 out of 100 take about 4 seconds or longer. That's more than four times the average, and those users notice.

This is why teams compare models and configs (their settings) on p95, not the average.

**Why "About 1 in 20 requests feels slow" is better:** 5 out of 100 is 1 in 20, so it describes what real users experience instead of an average that no single request may actually take.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Model B: its average is lower”?
check:1:1.a:
"Model B: its average is lower" gets one thing right. B's average really is a little lower. On a typical request, B is about as quick as A.

What it misses is the slow tail. An average blends every time into one number, so a few very slow requests barely move it. Model B's p95 is 6 seconds. That means about 5 out of 100 requests take 6 seconds or longer. In a chat, someone who sends 20 messages would likely hit one of those waits. A 6-second pause feels like the app is broken, and people remember it.

Model A's average is almost the same as B's. But its p95 is 2 seconds, so 95 out of 100 requests finish within 2 seconds. Its slow replies are much less painful.

"Model A: its p95 is much lower" is better because 95 out of 100 of A's requests come back within 2 seconds, while about 5 in 100 of B's take 6 seconds or more, and those long waits are what users feel.

judge.notes: No major problem. The line "on a typical request, B is about as quick as A" is inferred from averages, which the lesson says can hide slow requests, but it is plausible and not wrong.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Neither: the averages are close”?
check:1:2.a:
"Neither: the averages are close" gets one thing right. The averages really are close: 1 second versus just under 1 second. If you only looked at averages, the two models would seem the same.

What it misses is the lesson's big idea: **averages hide slow requests.** An average blends many fast replies with a few slow ones, so the slow ones get smoothed away.

The p95 numbers show what the averages hide. **p95** is the time that 95 out of 100 requests finish within.

- Model A: 95 out of 100 replies arrive in 2 seconds or less.
- Model B: you only get that same promise at 6 seconds. So B's slower replies take around three times as long as A's.

In a chat app, people remember the waits. Staring at a blank reply for about 6 seconds feels broken, even if most other replies were quick. B's slightly better average can't make up for that.

"Model A: its p95 is much lower" is better because it judges the models on the slow requests users actually notice, not on an average that hides them.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Only the model call, more often”?
check:2:0.a:
"Only the model call, more often" gets one thing right. Timing many requests is better than timing one. A single timing can be lucky or unlucky. You need lots of timings to work out p95, the time that 95 out of 100 requests finish within.

But it keeps timing the wrong thing. The model call takes 1 second, and users wait 5 seconds. So about 4 seconds go somewhere else, such as retrieval (looking up documents) or tool calls. Timing the model call more often just gives you more numbers that all leave out those 4 seconds. Your p95 would look fine while users still wait.

Instead, measure end-to-end latency: the whole request, from start to end. In MLflow, a trace is the record of every step one request went through. The trace's total duration gives you that end-to-end time. The individual steps recorded inside the trace then show where the extra 4 seconds went.

"The whole request, start to end" is better because it times what users actually wait for, not just one piece of it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Only the slowest model call”?
check:2:2.a:
"Only the slowest model call" gets one thing right. It looks for the slow part, and slow parts are what users notice.

But it still only looks at model calls. A request does more than call a model. It may do **retrieval** (looking up documents to give the model) and run **tools** (small helper programs, like a search or a database lookup). Each of those takes time too.

Look at the numbers in the question. The model call takes 1 second. Users wait 5 seconds. So about 4 seconds are spent somewhere else. Picking the slowest model call can't show you where. It might even be the same 1-second call you already timed.

There's a second problem. If a request makes several model calls, the slowest one shows only part of their time, not the total.

"The whole request, start to end" is better because it measures exactly what the user waits for, every step included. In MLflow, that is the trace's total duration.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Handle edge cases first” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Edge cases are the odd inputs at the boundaries: an empty list, a list with one item, or values you didn't expect. Your main logic is usually written with a "normal" list in mind. Edge cases are where that picture breaks.

In real work, these inputs show up more than you'd think. Say a new agent has had no traffic yet, or you filter traces to a quiet hour. `mlflow.search_traces` comes back with nothing, so `durations` is an empty list. There is no p95 of zero requests. If your function doesn't plan for that, it will likely crash with an `IndexError`, which is Python's error for asking for a list position that doesn't exist. Now the dashboard or nightly report that calls it fails too.

A one-item list is worth checking as well. With one request, every percentile should just be that request's time.

So before writing the main steps, decide what each odd input should do. For an empty list, that might mean returning `None` or raising a clear error. Writing that check first means a quiet hour is handled on purpose instead of breaking whatever depends on your function.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs the idea was skipped**

- Your average looks fine, but users still say it feels slow. The average is hiding the slow requests.
- Your latency number is lower than the total durations your MLflow traces show. You may be timing one step, not the whole request (end-to-end).
- One setup "wins" by a gap smaller than the spread between your passes. That gap is just noise.

**Signs your `percentile` function is wrong**

- **Off-by-one:** the most common bug. Python counts list places from 0, so position 3 is the third item. Mix up position and place, and you get the next value up. Often your p95 equals the slowest time, or p100 crashes with "index out of range."
- **No sorting:** p95 changes between runs on the same data.
- **Rounding down instead of up:** p95 comes out slightly too low.

**Quickest check**

Try a tiny list you can work out by hand, like the numbers 1 to 20, shuffled. The p95 should be 19, and the p100 should be 20. If you get 20 for p95, it is the off-by-one bug.

judge.notes: Two claims are shaky: an off-by-one gives only the next value up, so p95 equals the slowest time only on tiny lists (not 1,000 traces), and a missing sort changes p95 only if the input order changes, not 'on the same data'.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where p95 of end-to-end time needs extra care.

**Very little data.** With only 20 requests, p95 is the second-slowest one. One unlucky request can swing the number a lot. Collect a few hundred traces before you trust it, and report how many requests it came from.

**Things change over time.** If you pull traces from a whole month, old and new behaviour get mixed together. A new model, a config change, or a busy hour can hide inside one big number. Compare p95 over matching time windows, such as per day, and split it by model or config.

**Streaming LLM apps.** Streaming means the answer appears bit by bit as the model writes it. Users feel the wait before the first words more than the total time. So also track time to first token (a token is a small chunk of text, often part of a word), not just the trace's total duration.

learn:term.a:
**Latency** is the waiting time. It is how long a request takes to come back after someone sends it.

Think of ordering coffee. Latency is the gap between paying and getting your cup. You don't care which step was slow, the grinding or the milk. You just feel the total wait.

Here it is the same for an AI agent. A user asks a question. The agent might search documents (retrieval), call tools, and call the model. **End-to-end latency** is the full wait across all of those steps together. That's the one users feel.

It's usually measured in milliseconds (ms). 1,000 ms is one second.

In the lesson's example, latency shows up in each trace. A trace is MLflow's record of every step one request went through. Its total time is the latency.

- `trace.execution_time_ms > 5000` finds traces where the whole request took over 5,000 ms (5 seconds).
- `traces["execution_duration"]` gives each trace's total time in milliseconds.

Those numbers are the latencies you'll later sort through to find p95.
